title: What Makes Up the Cost of a Kilimanjaro Climb
excerpt: Park fees, crew, food, equipment and transfers: this is where the money for a Kilimanjaro climb goes, and why very cheap climbs should make you ask questions.
body:
When people compare Kilimanjaro offers, the differences can be large. It helps to know what you are actually paying for.

## Park fees

A large part of every climb goes to Kilimanjaro National Park: daily conservation fees, camping or hut fees, a rescue fee and VAT. These are set by the park authority and are the same for every operator. Because they are charged per day, a longer route costs more in fees. That is one reason an eight-day climb is more expensive than six days.

## The crew

A climber is usually supported by a lead guide, assistant guides, a cook and several porters. Fair wages, proper meals, warm clothing and safe loads for the crew cost money. This is where cheap operators most often cut corners. Read more in [porter welfare on Kilimanjaro](/blog/kilimanjaro-porter-welfare/).

## Food and equipment

Fresh food carried up the mountain, a mess tent, quality sleeping tents, a toilet tent, oximeters, a first-aid kit and emergency oxygen are part of a responsible climb.

## Transfers and nights before and after

Airport pick-up, the drive to the gate and hotel nights in Moshi or Arusha before and after the climb are usually included in a full package. Check this when comparing.

## What is not included

Usually flights, visa, travel insurance, personal gear, drinks in the hotel and tips for the crew are not included. Our [tipping guide](/blog/kilimanjaro-tipping-guide-crew/) explains how tipping works.

## Our prices

Prices depend on route, number of days, group size and season. We only quote a price after our partner Kilimanjaro Nature Tours has confirmed it for your dates. [Ask for a proposal](/travel-proposal/) and you will see exactly what is included.
